lesson.title: Cognitive Biases
lesson.summary: Mental shortcuts that distort our perception of reality — and how to minimize their impact on decisions.

blocks.text: Cognitive biases are systematic patterns of deviation from logical reasoning. Our brain uses shortcuts (heuristics) to save energy — but these shortcuts often distort reality.

items: Confirmation bias: seeking information that confirms what we already believe
Anchoring effect: giving excessive weight to the first piece of information received
Survivorship bias: analyzing only cases that 'survived', ignoring those that failed
Dunning-Kruger effect: overestimating one's own competence in areas of little knowledge

blocks.text: The first principle is not to fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool. — Richard Feynman
Seeking opposing perspectives, deciding with data, questioning your certainties, and using decision checklists are strategies that reduce the impact of biases.

cards.back: The tendency to seek, interpret, and remember information that confirms our pre-existing beliefs, while ignoring contrary evidence.
Focusing on cases that succeeded while ignoring those that failed, creating a distorted view of actual probabilities.
The tendency to be overly influenced by the first piece of information received when making decisions.

quiz.question: You only read news from sources that agree with your opinions. Which bias is at work?
quiz.explanation: Confirmation bias: seeking and valuing information that confirms what we already believe, while avoiding contrary information.

quiz.question: An investor only studies success stories of entrepreneurs. Which bias is distorting their analysis?
quiz.explanation: Survivorship bias: analyzing only successful cases ignores the majority that failed, distorting the true perception of risk.
